title: The Canada Border Services Agency crosses the line; Extraordinary powers
article: "A President once said, 'The only thing we have to fear is fear itself.' Now, we're supposed to be afraid. It's patriotic, in fact, and colourcoded." - from the song A Few Words in Defense of Our Country, by Randy Newman.

Let's call it for what it was, a coverup, because it took a month - and only after a breaking story in the media - before the Canada Border Services Agency fessed up to the death of Lucia Vega Jimenez, the Mexican woman who died of attempted suicide on their watch.

Even then it was a terse fessing up. The answers its hired flaks offered to the press in response to questions surrounding Jimenez's death could be translated as, "We'll get back to you." The CBSA played it close to its bulletproof vest, and offered nothing it didn't have to.

This is the go-to position in the new post 9 /11 world. Bogeymen in dark shades do their work out of the light of public scrutiny. We are to understand that, trust them, they're doing it for our own good, for our protection.
If it means taking liberties with our liberties in the name of liberty, well, then, that isn't a bad thing - it's just proof of the degree of threat that exists out there. It's justifiable paranoia.
The CBSA was formed in 2003 in the spirit of that paranoia. It was felt, most especially by the Americans, that our borders were too porous.

But in creating the CBSA, the government gave it extraordinary powers. Border services officers can arrest foreign nationals without a warrant. They can order their detention, and often send them to prisons where they are treated like other inmates. But once in custody, CBSA has a duty to ensure the health and safety of its detainees. This it failed to do with Jimenez.
These are not necessarily bad powers, given the job the CBSA has been created to do.

But they can be open to abuse, and the one thing that distinguishes the CBSA from all of our government's security and police forces is the fact that it operates with complete freedom. Unlike for the RCMP, there is no independent oversight of the activities of its officers. There is no formal complaint process or review of the conduct of CBSA officers. Injuries caused in the line of duty, or even death? It's all kept inhouse, despite demands for reform to the contrary.

"It has been seven years since the Arar Inquiry recommended that the CBSA be subjected to independent review," said Josh Paterson, executive director of the B.C. Civil Liberties Association. "And for seven years there has been no action."

Paterson was part of a civil rights coalition that in a press conference Wednesday called for the establishment of an independent body to oversee the practices of the CBSA. The Arar Inquiry he referred to came about after Maher Arar, a telecommunications engineer with dual Canadian and Syrian citizenship, was detained while travelling in the U.S. He was held under suspicion of being a terrorist, and was sent to Syria. There, he was tortured. After his release, he returned to Canada. The inquiry exonerated him and the Canadian government apologized for the role it played in his detainment.
But Arar's case and the Jimenez case, Paterson said, aren't exceptions. They're only the most visible.

"While (Jimenez's) death in custody was unusual," he said, "there is nothing unusual about allegations of abuse of power, negligent policing or unfair treatment by the CBSA. We at the BCCLA, and lawyers across Canada, hear story after story of this kind of abuse."

Some of it, the civil rights groups say, is just clumsy police work on the part of the CBSA that, by sharing information with other governments or certain individuals, can put the detainee's life at risk once they are returned to their country of origin.

These civil rights groups aren't saying that refugee claimants shouldn't be scrutinized. But it shouldn't be the task of the CBSA, they say, it should be the Immigration and Refugee Board, which has procedures in place for gathering evidence that doesn't expose claimants or their families to danger.
Refugees expose themselves to enough risk by trying to enter Canada. Many are legitimate, some are not, and the public wants a border agency that maintains our borders' integrity.
